title: Subgroup deployment-readiness audit of calibration and clinical utility in perioperative infection prediction.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] We audited deployment readiness of an end-of-surgery postoperative infection model across clinically relevant subgroups and assessed mitigation of subgroup miscalibration. We analyzed out-of-fold predictions from 10 719 procedures (2014-2022) with 504 present-on-admission (POA)-coded postoperative infection events across recorded sex, age, and a clinical physiological-reserve proxy. We assessed discrimination, calibration, threshold-specific errors, and decision-curve net benefit, treating t = 0.10 as a reference anchor. We compared no recalibration with common and group-specific cross-fitted isotonic recalibration, evaluated a refit without the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), and performed a temporal-holdout analysis. Overall area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.876, with similar sex-marginal discrimination in women and men (0.878 vs 0.875). Calibration-in-the-large was -1.02 overall, -0.86 in frail, and -1.34 in prefrail patients; the 6-event nonfrail stratum was not estimable. At t = 0.10, net benefit was positive in frail and negative in prefrail patients in the source cohort, but negative prefrail utility did not persist in the ascertainable-period (2018-2022) and temporal analyses. Common recalibration moved overall calibration-in-the-large from -1.020 to -0.007. Removing SMOTE shifted overall calibration but did not reduce the reserve gradient. Temporal-holdout AUROC was 0.851 with persistent overprediction. Present-on-admission coding was effectively absent before 2018; prevalence-dependent results were therefore additionally reported for the ascertainable 2018-2022 period, and ascertainment differed by physiological reserve. Discrimination-only or sex-marginal evaluation would have missed deployment-relevant subgroup heterogeneity, while endpoint ascertainment affected prevalence-dependent interpretation. Joint subgroup evaluation can identify deployment-relevant limitations missed by aggregate metrics. Prospective validation with comparable outcome ascertainment remains necessary before clinical deployment.

title: [Articles] An explainable artificial intelligence system for prognostic assessment and decision support in diabetic foot ulcer care: a multicentre derivation and validation study with prospective randomised evaluation
desc: We demonstrate that integrating gradient-boosted trees and neural networks enables explainable prediction of complex DFU trajectories and may support prioritised, individualised clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, recurrence estimates should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Facelift Surgery: A Systematic Review of Objective Outcome Assessment and Patient-Perceived Rejuvenation.
desc: [Aesthetic plastic surgery] Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a tool for objective outcome assessment in facelift surgery (rhytidectomy), yet the clinical validity and limitations of these technologies remain incompletely characterized. This review evaluates the evidence on AI applications in facelift surgery, focusing on neural network based age estimation, concordance with patient perception, and large language model (LLM) supported patient counseling. A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Databases were searched for studies applying AI to facelift surgery with primary clinical data. Nine studies published between 2020 and 2025 met inclusion criteria. Convolutional neural networks quantified postoperative age reduction ranging from 1.7 to 5.8 years depending on surgical technique and follow-up interval. AI-derived estimates consistently underestimated patient-perceived rejuvenation by approximately 35% to 50%. Superficial musculoaponeurotic system-based techniques demonstrated greater AI-measured age reduction than skin-only procedures. LLMs achieved 85% to 88% diagnostic accuracy for patient counseling but exceeded recommended readability standards. AI enables objective quantification of facelift outcomes but demonstrates systematic discordance with patient perception. Current AI modalities should function as adjuncts to validated patient-reported outcome measures, not replacements. These preliminary findings warrant cautious interpretation given the limited and heterogeneous evidence base. Ethical concerns regarding algorithmic definitions of surgical success warrant consideration. This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 .

title: Machine Learning Based Detection of Chronic Kidney Disease using Full Blood Count from a Ghanaian Hospital Population with an Integrated Web Application
desc: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is usually silent until advanced, and the tests confirming it are frequently unaffordable in sub-Saharan Africa, whereas the full blood count (FBC) is inexpensive and widely performed. We assessed whether machine learning applied to the FBC can detect CKD, and how far its reported performance depends on where synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) is applied. Records of 155 patients at the Ho Technical University Hospital, Ghana, 43 (27.7%) with CKD, yielded ten features: age, cardiovascular disease and eight raw FBC parameters. Eleven algorithms, six resampling strategies and thirteen ensembles were compared under repeated stratified cross-validation. With SMOTE applied before the train-test split, the protocol under which the deployed models were fitted, Random Forest and Extra Trees both reached an accuracy of 83.9%, with sensitivities of 0.893 and 0.857 and areas under the curve (AUC) of 0.925 and 0.939; repeated cross-validation gave an accuracy of 0.809 {+/-} 0.051 and an AUC of 0.897. With resampling confined to the training folds, the same features gave a held-out accuracy of 61.5% and an AUC of 0.604 in 39 unseen patients. Age was the only variable separating the groups after correction for multiple testing (median 64 versus 47 years, adjusted p = 0.0026). The models are deployed as NephroScan GH (https://nephroscangh.com), which explains every prediction. The FBC carries a real but moderate signal for CKD, and the 22.4 point gap between the two protocols quantifies how far a single preprocessing decision can move a reported accuracy.

title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models
desc: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.

External validation and clinical implementation of clinical prediction models: a systematic review.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To assess whether external validation and clinical implementation of clinical prediction models reflect sequential or distinct stages of a translational pathway. This cross-sectional meta-epidemiologic study analyzed 1072 machine learning-based clinical prediction models published across clinical domains (2017-2019). We assessed downstream external validation and clinical implementation via citation screening through August 2025. Evaluated exposures included public code availability, TRIPOD adherence, multicenter design, and sample size. Secondary outcomes included investigator overlap. Among 1072 studies, 88.1% lacked translational follow-up. Only 9.9% underwent external validation, and 5.2% reached clinical implementation. Code availability (odds ratio [OR] 3.04; 95% CI, 1.91-4.84) and higher TRIPOD adherence (OR 2.68 per 10% increase; 95% CI, 2.04-3.52) were significantly associated with external validation, but not consistently with clinical implementation. Notably, 39% of implemented models lacked prior external validation. Independent groups predominantly conducted external validation (72.6%), whereas implementation frequently involved original development teams. Findings indicate a divergence in algorithmic translation. Characteristics emphasizing evaluability (code availability, reporting transparency) facilitate external validation but do not ensure clinical implementation. The frequent bypass of independent validation before implementation highlights a reliance on institutional and operational factors rather than generalizable methodology. External validation and clinical implementation appear to represent distinct translational processes rather than sequential stages influenced by a uniform set of factors. Current practices facilitate validation but inadequately address operational requirements for real-world deployment.

title: Trigger-first large language model-assisted adverse drug reaction surveillance: A pharmacist-supervised retrospective cohort study.
source: PubMed · Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
desc: [Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy] Active pharmacovigilance in low-prevalence settings requires review of large electronic health record cohorts. We evaluated a pharmacist-supervised workflow combining electronic triggers with large language model (LLM)-assisted review. To assess candidate enrichment and stage-specific performance for adverse drug reaction (ADR) surveillance. In this retrospective cohort study, two pharmacists established a blinded reference standard for 7950 exposure episodes from 7950 unique inpatients. A prespecified Chinese Hospital Pharmacovigilance System trigger selected candidates for Qwen3-4B-Instruct and an institution-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-fine-tuned model trained on 410 patient-disjoint cases involving other medicines. Paired errors were compared using exact McNemar tests. Twenty-eight episodes were ADR-positive. The trigger selected 167 candidates (2.10%), with 100.0% sensitivity (95% confidence interval, 87.66-100.0%) and 98.25% specificity. For the base versus LoRA-fine-tuned model, sensitivity was 82.14% versus 92.86%, specificity 88.49% versus 94.96%, positive predictive value 58.97% versus 78.79%, and F1 score 68.66% versus 85.25%. LoRA reduced false positives from 16 to 7 (9 corrected, 0 new; P = 0.0039). The numerical increase in sensitivity was not statistically significant (P = 0.250), with only 28 ADR-positive episodes available for evaluation. Trigger-first screening reduced review volume, while LoRA fine-tuning improved false-positive control. LLM classifications should support pharmacist review and should not be used as an autonomous exclusion rule.

title: EMBER: Contextualized gene representations enable compositional prediction across cellular perturbations
desc: Predicting the effects of individual and combined perturbations is central to identifying context-specific vulnerabilities and designing targeted interventions. Yet learning gene representations that integrate functional relationships with cellular state and transfer across perturbation tasks remains challenging. Here, we present EMBER, a gene-centric foundation model that learns context-dependent functional representations of genes. EMBER combines interaction-guided contrastive learning with masked expression reconstruction during pretraining on a single-cell corpus curated for diversity and balanced sampling across cell types and experimental batches. EMBER decouples gene representation learning from task-specific prediction through a composable embedding framework: the pretrained encoder remains frozen, while lightweight probes combine contextualized gene embeddings to predict individual and combined perturbation effects. The same pretrained representations support single-gene perturbation-response prediction, digenic interaction prediction, and multi-target drug-response prediction. EMBER improves cross-context perturbation-response prediction and genetic-interaction ranking relative to evaluated baselines. EMBER also prioritized SCFD1, a mediator of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as a candidate dependency during mTOR inhibition. Together, these results establish contextualized gene embeddings as reusable building blocks for modeling genetic and pharmacological perturbations, supporting the prioritization of genetic interactions and context-specific interventions for experimental testing.

An uncertainty-aware deep learning-based registration model for adaptive lung cancer radiotherapy.
source: PubMed · Physics in medicine and biology
desc: [Physics in medicine and biology] To develop a deep learning (DL) based probabilistic 3D deformable image registration framework for uncertainty-aware dose accumulation in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) of lung cancer. Approach: We propose TransMorph-prob (TM-prob), a variational Bayesian model that predicts the voxel-wise mean and variance of dense displacement fields (DDFs). Two TM-prob models were trained on an internal CT dataset (725 patients) and a low-field MR-linac dataset (102 patients), and benchmarked against Monte Carlo dropout TransMorph (TM-MCD) and DIRUncertainty with B-spline initialization (ASDIR) on the DIRLAB 4DCT dataset (10 patients, 3000 landmarks), and an annotated MR-linac dataset (16 patients, 107 image pairs, 227 landmarks) with target and seven organ-at-risk (OAR) contours. Both datasets contained an additional 1239/13,289 algorithm-generated landmarks. Performance was evaluated using target registration error (TRE), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), landmark- and voxel-wise expected calibration errors (LECE/ECE), and dose distributions derived from 2000 DDF samples per patient. Main results: On the DIRLAB dataset, TM-prob achieved a median TRE of \qty{1.8}{\mm}/\qty{2.8}{\mm} on manual/algorithm-generated landmarks, versus \qty{1.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.4}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{2.1}{\mm}/\qty{3.0}{\mm} for TM-MCD. On the MRI dataset, TM-prob achieved the median TRE of \qty{3.9}{\mm}/\qty{2.6}{\mm} and a mean DSC of 0.87, matching ASDIR (\qty{3.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.7}{\mm}, and DSC of 0.87) while outperforming TM-MCD (\qty{4.4}{\mm}/\qty{2.9}{\mm}, and 0.84). In uncertainty calibration, TM-prob achieved a LECE of \qty{1.74}{\mm}/\qty{0.30}{\mm} on MRI manual/algorithm-generated landmarks versus \qty{2.41}{\mm}/\qty{0.56}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{6.65}{\mm}/\qty{3.92}{\mm} for TM-MCD, and an average contour ECE of 5.8% versus 7.0% and 21.2%. Two patients with indistinct GTV boundaries exhibited substantially wider target D95 distributions, demonstrating that calibrated DDF uncertainty translates into clinically relevant dose-coverage uncertainty. Significance: TM-prob is an end-to-end DL model, achieving fast, well-calibrated, uncertainty-aware registration for lung cancer patients, enabling reliable DDF uncertainty propagation into dose accumulation for clinical decision-making in online adaptive radiotherapy.

title: A comprehensive map of the sequence basis of transcription initiation in humans
desc: Transcription initiation is a key marker of active enhancers and promoters. Here we describe an atlas of efficient and interpretable deep learning models trained on over 200 transcription initiation profiling experiments representing all major human organs and many cancer types. We show that our models accurately predict initiation patterns from local DNA sequence and decode their sequence determinants across diverse cellular contexts.

A Large Language Model Framework for Seed Implant Brachytherapy: Adaptive Weight Optimization via Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
source: PubMed · Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
desc: [Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences] Seed implant brachytherapy (SIBT) is an effective cancer treatment modality; however, clinical planning often relies on manual adjustment of objective function weights, leading to inefficiencies and suboptimal results. This study proposes an adaptive weight optimization framework for SIBT planning, driven by large language models (LLMs). A locally deployed DeepSeek-R1 LLM is integrated with an automatic planning algorithm in an iterative loop. Starting with fixed weights, the LLM evaluates plan quality and recommends new weights in the next iteration. This process continues until convergence criteria are met, after which the LLM conducts a comprehensive evaluation to identify the optimal plan. A clinical knowledge base, constructed and queried via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), enhances the model's domain-specific reasoning. The proposed method was retrospectively validated on 23 patient cases who underwent head-and-neck SIBT, showing that the LLM-assisted approach maintained clinical target volume (CTV) coverage and reduced excessive target dose relative to fixed-weight planning; in the eight patients with available organs at risk (OARs) contours, OAR dose metrics showed favorable numerical trends. The study demonstrates the potential of LLMs as assistive tools for SIBT planning under clinician supervision.

title: Agentic cryo-EM structure determination with CryoPilot
desc: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo EM) relies on mature computational tools, but experts must still inspect intermediate results, choose among alternative processing routes, and decide when earlier choices should be revised. Here we present CryoPilot, a system of two language model agents that carries cryo-EM data from raw micrographs through three-dimensional reconstruction to validated atomic models. Rather than executing a predefined pipeline, its reconstruction agent evaluates intermediate images and quantitative diagnostics, selects and parameterizes CryoSPARC jobs, tests alternative strategies, compares their outcomes, and retains, revises, or reverts decisions accordingly. A persistent programming environment and session database preserve the complete processing history, making each decision traceable and allowing multi day workflows to proceed with minimal human intervention. Its modeling agent determines map handedness, builds atomic models with CryoZeta, removes regions the density does not support, and optimizes each model by testing refinement steps against map fit, geometry, and DAQ, a measure of local model to map agreement. Across nine public EMPIAR datasets, eight reconstructions reached 2.61 to 3.51 A resolution, and refined models from seven maps agreed with reference structures to within 0.4 to 4.9 A Calpha; RMSD. For a challenging alpha latrocrustotoxin dataset, a single change of particle picking strategy that we suggested enabled CryoPilot to improve the reconstruction from 5.9 to 4.15 A. CryoPilot establishes an adaptive and auditable framework for agent-driven cryo-EM structure determination.

Artificial intelligence across the gastric cancer care continuum: Clinical evidence, multimodal integration, and translation.
desc: [iScience] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across the gastric cancer care continuum, but its clinical maturity differs substantially among endoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, digital pathology, prognostic modeling, treatment selection, and surgical support. Existing reviews have often focused on individual modalities or summarized algorithmic performance without systematically distinguishing technical feasibility from translational readiness. We conducted a structured narrative review of studies indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection from January 2022 through July 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Earlier landmark studies were retained when necessary to explain the development of major applications. Priority was given to prospective, multicenter, externally validated, and clinically actionable studies. Evidence maturity was assessed according to study design, validation breadth, workflow relevance, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, and implementation evidence. The main constraint on gastric cancer AI is no longer pattern-recognition capability but the absence of reproducible clinical benefit under real-world conditions. Priorities include multiregional prospective validation, standardized calibration and decision curve assessment, comparison of clinicians with and without AI, integration into existing workflows, evaluation of economic and patient-level outcomes, and post-deployment monitoring.

title: Mechanistic gene-regulation-based trajectory inference with bowside
desc: While single-cell RNA sequencing enables the in-depth study of differentiation processes, simultaneous trajectory inference and gene regulatory network reconstruction remain challenging. We propose bowside, a shallow neural stochastic differentiation model that mechanistically models gene regulation. Our method successfully recovers gene expression trends and the underlying regulatory interactions. We demonstrate bowside on hematopoiesis and induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming data, retrieving known fate-determining network motifs.

Virology-aware artificial intelligence for respiratory antiviral discovery: from molecular docking biases to RdRp-centered benchmarking.
desc: [Frontiers in pharmacology] Respiratory RNA viruses remain a persistent threat because they combine high transmissibility, rapid evolution, immune escape, zoonotic spillover, and incomplete therapeutic coverage. RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRps) and polymerase complexes are among the most conserved and pharmacologically actionable viral targets, yet they are also challenging computational targets because their ligandable states depend on RNA templates, cofactors, divalent metals, multidomain architecture, and conformational transitions. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), geometric deep learning (GDL), and generative molecular design are increasingly used to accelerate antiviral discovery, yet their performance is often inferred from general protein-ligand benchmarks dominated by non-viral targets. This review argues that respiratory RNA virus polymerases are a high-value but comparatively underrepresented class of antiviral targets and a complementary test case for evaluating AI-guided drug discovery. We synthesize current approaches in computer-aided drug design (CADD), molecular docking, ML-assisted virtual screening, molecular representations, pose-generation models, generative AI, and protein-ligand affinity benchmarking. We emphasize that docking scores, predicted affinity, and root-mean-square error (RMSE) values are insufficient unless linked to target engagement, enzymatic inhibition, cell-based antiviral activity, cytotoxicity, resistance, and pharmacological feasibility. We propose an RdRp-centered AI pipeline that integrates curated polymerase structural ensembles, leakage-resistant benchmarking, antiviral-specific evaluation tasks, ADME/Tox filtering, biochemical validation, cell-based infection assays, resistance profiling, and iterative model refinement. Moving beyond docking scores requires benchmarking models under virologically realistic conditions and validating whether computational prioritization enriches compounds with experimentally actionable antiviral activity.

title: Task-Dependent Performance of GNNs and Pretrained Models in ADMET Prediction
desc: Structure-based prediction of ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) properties promises fast, low-cost screening of drug candidates, yet model selection remains unclear because published comparisons of molecular representations often use unmatched tuning budgets and leakage-prone evaluation protocols, producing performance differences that may not reflect model quality. To address this gap, we benchmark graph neural networks (GNNs), frozen pretrained models (ChemBERTa, MolCLR), and fingerprint baselines across six Therapeutics Data Commons ADMET endpoints under scaffold-split evaluation. To make it really fair we gave every model family a matched 50-trial, validation-selected tuning budget and reported the median over ten seeds; architecture and hyperparameter selection use validation data only, with the held-out test split reserved for final performance estimation. Under this fair comparison protocol, emph{no model family dominates} and the differences between families fall within the seed-to-seed range on most endpoints. The GNN is clearly best only on Caco-2 permeability (R$^2 approx 0.48$), and a controlled ablation shows this advantage comes entirely from auxiliary physicochemical descriptors rather than the graph representation; Morgan fingerprints are competitive on hERG (AUC $approx 0.77$) and give the best median on both clearance endpoints, while MolCLR is best on Tox21. For hepatocyte clearance and half-life, all models yield near-zero or negative R$^2$. No single hyperparameter-optimization strategy, among seven evaluated, consistently outperforms random search at this budget, and we show that selecting the optimizer using test-set performance or reporting only single best-trial runs can substantially inflate a favored model's apparent advantage. Reliable ADMET modeling therefore requires endpoint-specific model selection together with fair, leakage-controlled, seed-averaged evaluation, offering more trustworthy decision support for early-stage drug candidate prioritization.

Machine learning and deep learning for diagnosis of endometriosis: systematic review and meta-analysis.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] To assess the diagnostic accuracy of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models for endometriosis. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251231469). Databases were searched through November 24, 2025. Twenty-two eligible studies were included. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Pooled analysis was conducted in Stata 18.0. Pooled sensitivity was 0.90 (95% CI 0.86-0.93), specificity 0.75 (95% CI 0.64-0.84), and SROC-AUC 0.92 (95% CI 0.89-0.94). A positive prediction increased disease probability from 10% to 29%, whereas a negative prediction reduced it to 1%. Multicenter design and DL were associated with lower sensitivity. Results were robust. ML/DL models demonstrate high diagnostic performance and are promising for non-invasive auxiliary diagnosis. Large multicenter prospective studies and multimodal models are needed to enable clinical translation.Systematic Review Registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251231469, identifier CRD420251231469.

title: Artificial intelligence-enabled detection of vascular perfusion defects on ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy for pulmonary embolism.
source: PubMed · Physics in medicine and biology
desc: [Physics in medicine and biology] Accurate interpretation of planar ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, used for diagnosing pulmonary embolism (PE) based on PIOPED/EANM guidelines, requires objective assessment of mismatched V/Q defects. Manual delineation of V/Q defects is time-consuming, subject to interobserver variability, and rarely performed in practice, limiting standardized reporting and quantification of disease burden. To address these challenges, we evaluated four modern AI models for automated segmentation of vascular perfusion defects in planar V/Q scans and compared their performance to human annotators. We retrospectively identified 2,118 patients who underwent planar V/Q scans at The Ottawa Hospital (June 2019-February 2023). Six standard projections (ANT, POST, LAO, RAO, LPO, RPO) were included. Four 2D neural networks (U-Net, nnU-Net, Swin UNETR, and a Bottleneck Transformer U-Net [BTU-Net]) were trained on 1,313 patients (7,878 projections) and validated on 329 (1,974 projections) using physician-annotated defects. A hold-out test set of 46 high probability patients was used to evaluate segmentation quality, and defect detection accuracy using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) analysis. BTU-Net was the only model performing on par with human readers, showing robust sensitivity across the entire range of segmentation probabilities. At 1.5 false positives per projection rate (FPPR), BTU-Net outperformed other models with sensitivity of 0.529 ± 0.026, On a separate hold-out set of low likelihood of disease patients (n=430), the lowest FPPR was 0.08 ± 0.01 for BTU-Net (P<0.0001). BTU-Net enables rapid, consistent, and accurate interpretation of planar V/Q scans. Such tools may enhance diagnostic efficiency, standardize reporting, and support non-expert readers in evaluating PE.

title: Artificial intelligence in health insurance fraud detection: a global and regional systematic review.
desc: [Frontiers in public health] Health insurance fraud imposes substantial financial burdens on healthcare systems and reduces the efficiency of healthcare resource utilization worldwide. Traditional fraud detection approaches often struggle to analyse large and complex healthcare claims data, making artificial intelligence (AI) an increasingly important tool for identifying fraudulent activities. This study systematically reviews global and regional evidence on AI applications in health insurance fraud detection, with particular emphasis on methodological approaches, performance evaluation, and implementation challenges. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Seven electronic databases were searched for studies published between 2016 and 2025. Titles and abstracts were screened using the Silvi AI platform, followed by eligibility assessment according to pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted using a standardized framework, and methodological quality was assessed using the Drummond 10-item checklist. From 450 identified records, 33 studies met the eligibility criteria. The included studies demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in datasets, AI methodologies, fraud types, and performance evaluation metrics. Machine learning was the most frequently applied approach, followed by deep learning, graph-based learning, and hybrid AI frameworks. Although AI-based methods consistently improved fraud detection performance, challenges related to dataset imbalance, standardized reporting, interpretability, external validation, and economic evaluation remain significant barriers to widespread implementation. AI demonstrates considerable potential for improving health insurance fraud detection. However, future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, explainable AI, external validation across diverse healthcare systems, and economic assessment to support the responsible and scalable deployment of AI-enabled fraud detection systems.

title: Artificial intelligence for medication recognition and safety: a systematic review of detection, classification, OCR, and digital health applications.
desc: [Frontiers in digital health] Medication errors and adverse drug events remain causes of patient harm, underscoring the need for technologies supporting medication identification, verification, and medication safety. Artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, optical character recognition (OCR), and digital health technologies are applied to medication recognition. To systematically review AI-based medication recognition systems and characterize recognition tasks, computational approaches, datasets, evaluation, validation, generalizability, deployment, applications, and emerging directions. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and PubMed/MEDLINE were searched for publications from 1 January 2016 to 4 September 2026, using two conceptual blocks covering medication recognition and AI methods. Of 895 retrieved records, 136 duplicates were removed, and 759 records underwent screening. After full-text assessment, 14 reports were excluded, and 91 studies were included. Title-and-abstract screening yielded 84.72% observed agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.527 ). For methodological assessment, both reviewers independently applied D1-D8 to the 91 included studies before consensus resolution. Across 728 domain-level assessments, observed agreement was 97.66%, with an aggregate Cohen's κ of 0.959; domain-specific κ values ranged from 0.857 to 1.000. Evidence was synthesized through cross-study analysis and four evidence maps. Evidence shows use of detection, classification, OCR/imprint recognition, hybrid and multimodal architectures, alongside few-shot, low-shot, zero-shot, and incremental learning. Applications extend to assistive, mobile, and IoT-enabled systems, medication verification, and clinical decision support. Heterogeneity in datasets, imaging conditions, evaluation protocols, and validation strategies limits comparison and generalizability. External validation, cross-dataset testing, unseen-medication evaluation, prospective deployment, and clinical testing remain limited. AI-based medication recognition is evolving from a computer vision task into a digital informatics component supporting medication safety, accessibility, verification, and patient care. Future research should prioritize diverse datasets, leakage control, independent multicenter validation, unseen-medication evaluation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, interoperability, and resource-efficient deployment. title: Artificial intelligence innovations in low vision rehabilitation: a systematic review of emerging technologies.
desc: [Frontiers in digital health] Low vision is one of the major types of visual impairment worldwide and when diagnosed early can help with its management. Artificial intelligence (AI) has recently shown promising outcomes in all fields including health, with low vision rehabilitation being one of its significant applications. This systematic review aims to provide an up-to-date and comprehensive evaluation of the application of AI in the management of low vision. The systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. All relevant published papers were retrieved through searches from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore, without date restrictions. All retrieved articles from electronic databases were collated and managed in Covidence software. Nineteen studies were included, consisting of six application domains, which include assistive navigation and wayfinding (n = 8), environmental interaction and object recognition (n = 5), reading and text access (n = 2), educational accessibility (n = 1), medical applications (n = 3), and digital accessibility optimization (n = 1). Navigation systems demonstrated the strongest performance, with leading systems achieving sub-meter location error and 100% task success rates in real-world testing. Object recognition accuracies reached 97%, hazard detection achieved 92.0% dynamic accuracy with temporal filtering, and multimodal environmental understanding received risk assessment ratings of 9.40/10. Recurring technical limitations included sensitivity to lighting conditions, processing latency, and connectivity dependency. AI assistive technologies for low vision demonstrate technical feasibility with promising performance. However, important evidence gaps limit clinical application: the absence of prospective validation, limited comparative effectiveness data, and minimal patient-centered outcomes. Future studies should use standardized outcomes, larger and more diverse datasets, and longitudinal evaluations to demonstrate real-world impact. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261324781, CRD420261324781.

title: HER2 in solid tumors: microenvironment features and multifaceted advances from mechanisms to clinical translation.
desc: [Experimental hematology & oncology] Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a well-established oncogenic driver in multiple solid tumors, most prominently in breast and gastric cancers. Beyond gene amplification-driven signaling through canonical PI3K/AKT and RAS/MAPK pathways, emerging evidence reveals that HER2 functions within a highly dynamic and context-dependent tumor ecosystem. Interactions between HER2-positive tumor cells and immune and stromal compartments actively shape the tumor microenvironment, contributing to immune evasion, therapeutic resistance and disease progression. A central challenge in the clinical management of HER2-altered cancers is pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity, which undermines both diagnostic accuracy and the durability of targeted therapies. In response, advances in multi-omics profiling, liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted analytics are redefining HER2 assessment, shifting it from static tissue-based classification towards dynamic, minimally invasive monitoring. In parallel, the therapeutic landscape has evolved from single-agent HER2 blockade to rational combination strategies. In particular, antibody-drug conjugates have emerged as a transformative modality, extending the therapeutic reach of HER2 targeting beyond traditional indications and offering new opportunities to overcome heterogeneity and drug resistance. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular and microenvironmental biology of HER2-altered solid tumors and discusses how these advances are reshaping next-generation precision oncology.

title: Artificial intelligence-supported revision of nursing care plans in a standardised newborn vignette: a one-group pretest-posttest study.
source: PubMed · Journal of research in nursing : JRN
desc: [Journal of research in nursing : JRN] Nursing students often produce care plans that are plausible yet generic, with weak linkage among diagnoses, interventions and outcomes. Teacher-mediated, bounded generative AI may support revision while preserving clinical judgement. To assess whether an AI-supported Reflect-Compare-Revise workflow improves nursing care plan quality and diagnosis-intervention-outcome alignment using a standardised newborn vignette. A one-group pretest-posttest study involved 40 second-year nursing students at a public university in the Philippines. Students wrote an unaided care plan, then revised it using the structured workflow. Two blinded nurse-educator raters scored paired plans using the Quality of Diagnoses, Interventions and Outcomes instrument. Post-revision documentation quality improved across all domains, with the largest raw gains in diagnostic formulation and nursing-sensitive outcomes. Interventions and outcomes remained the weaker downstream domains, with outcomes lowest at posttest. Diagnosis-intervention-outcome alignment and specificity increased, although explicit cross-linking remained inconsistent. This study adds preliminary evidence for nursing education: higher scores after guided AI-supported revision were associated with clearer and more coherent clinical reasoning in care planning. Policy recommendations are to permit bounded AI use with standardised prompts, revision logs/checklists, rubric-based feedback and verification safeguards to protect documentation integrity and patient safety.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
desc: [Frontiers in oncology] Imaging-guided interventional radiotherapy (IG-IRT) is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer but remains time-consuming and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to improve efficiency and reproducibility. A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2010 and 2026 investigating AI-based imaging applications in cervical IRT. Eligible studies included original research evaluating segmentation (targets and organ at risk), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection. Fifty-two studies were included. Deep learning-based segmentation showed variable performance across anatomical structures and studies, with Dice coefficients approaching or exceeding 0.90 for some organs at risk and target volumes in the best-performing models. Individual studies reported shorter processing times, reduced contouring variability, accurate applicator reconstruction, and potential support for applicator selection. However, the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity precluded direct comparisons among AI approaches. The available studies suggest that AI may support the automation of selected workflow steps and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. While several applications have achieved high technical performance, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, and robust external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before routine clinical adoption.

title: Barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales: findings from focus groups.
desc: [Frontiers in digital health] Building on a previous Wales-wide survey, this study aimed to provide more in-depth exploration of the barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales. The study aimed to explore these barriers and facilitators among various social groups, to inform policy development in Wales. Four focus groups were conducted with a group of members of the public and a group of healthcare professionals (both groups recruited from a previous survey), as well as a group Sixth Form students and a group of retired adults. Inductive thematic analysis was used to generate themes and to compare the issues raised by the various groups. Contiguity-based analysis was undertaken to underscore how themes related with each other. A total of 21 individuals participated in the focus groups (healthcare professionals=6, members of the public=6, sixth-form students=5, retirees=4). Seven thematic networks were identified. Across groups, seven themes were identified in the healthcare professional group, six in the general members of the public group, seven in the sixth form student group, and seven in the retiree group. All groups voiced concerns about data privacy and highlighted the importance of human oversight of AI and human contact during the clinical encounter as they expressed more trust in human practitioners. There were though differences between groups, such as greater trust in black-box systems by healthcare professionals, and between individual participants in regard to trust in private organisations developing AI for healthcare organisations. All groups were concerned with information security and expressed a preference for human contact during the clinical encounter and a human-in-the-loop approach. There were differences between the groups, such as in attitudes towards black-box AI technologies and trust in clinicians. No additional barriers or facilitators were identified for proxy consent.

title: CT-based deep learning integrating pancreatic imaging and body composition for severity prediction in acute pancreatitis.
desc: [Insights into imaging] To develop and validate a deep learning (DL)-based CT model integrating pancreatic imaging and CT-derived body composition for severity prediction in acute pancreatitis (AP). In this retrospective dual-center study, patients with AP who underwent CT within 72 h of symptom onset were enrolled from January 2021 to September 2025 at Center 1 and January 2023 to September 2024 at Center 2. The primary dataset (n = 426) was randomly divided into a training set (n = 298) and an internal test set (n = 128), while 110 patients from Center 2 served as the external test set. A three-dimensional DL model was developed for pancreatic imaging, and two-dimensional DL models were constructed for L3-level visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and skeletal muscle (SM). Six predictive models were constructed: clinical, pancreas, VAT, SM, pancreas-clinical (PC), and combined. Performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis, DeLong testing, calibration, decision curve analysis, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). The combined model achieved area under the curve (AUCs) of 0.897 (95% CI: 0.862-0.932), 0.909 (95% CI: 0.861-0.958), and 0.910 (95% CI: 0.856-0.964) in the training, internal test, and external test sets, respectively. The combined model outperformed the PC model in the training set (p = 0.002) and external test set (p = 0.020). NRI and IDI analyses confirmed the incremental predictive value of body composition features. A CT-based DL model integrating pancreatic imaging, body composition, and clinical variables demonstrated good performance for AP severity prediction. Question Early severity stratification in AP remains challenging because conventional clinical and imaging assessments may not fully capture pancreatic injury and systemic disease status. Findings A CT-based DL model integrating pancreatic imaging, body composition, and clinical variables demonstrated good performance for severity prediction in AP. Critical Relevance Statement This study evaluates the value of integrating pancreatic imaging and CT-derived body composition information and supports the use of routinely acquired CT data for early risk stratification, potentially facilitating more individualized monitoring and management of AP.

title: Attitudes and perceptions toward artificial intelligence among practicing rheumatologists in Iraq: a cross-sectional web-based survey.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of healthcare, particularly in rheumatology, where clinicians must integrate complex clinical, laboratory, and imaging data. Physicians' perceptions of AI may substantially influence the extent to which it is implemented responsibly in routine clinical practice. This study aimed to assess the attitudes of practicing rheumatologists in Iraq toward artificial intelligence and to examine their association with demographic and professional characteristics. A four-month web-based cross-sectional survey was conducted from October 2025 to January 2026. A questionnaire adapted from previous studies was refined through expert review and pilot testing before distribution. The questionnaire comprised demographic information, attitude statements measured on a five-point Likert scale, and items assessing general perceptions of artificial intelligence. Composite attitude scores were categorized using modified Bloom's cutoff criteria. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS and R. A total of 162 complete responses were collected. Most respondents were aged 35-44 years (42.0%), male (56.8%), and specialists (67.9%). Overall, 61.7% reported familiarity with AI and 69.1% had already used AI in rheumatology practice. Most participants 56.8% exhibited a poor attitude, 32.1% a moderate attitude, and 11.1% a good attitude toward AI. Bivariate analysis identified familiarity with AI ( p = 0.003 ) and involvement in research ( p = 0.009 ) as significantly associated with more favorable attitudes. Iraqi rheumatologists demonstrate cautious engagement with artificial intelligence, with the majority displaying poor-to-moderate overall attitude scores on the standardized composite scale. Greater familiarity with AI and research involvement were associated with more favorable attitudes, highlighting the importance of targeted digital literacy and specialty-specific education to support effective AI adoption in clinical practice.

title: Artificial Intelligence-powered Advances in Phytomedicine: A Systematic Review on Plant-based Drug Discovery Software.
desc: [Current drug discovery technologies] Herbal medicines contain complex phytochemicals that offer therapeutic potential, but their long-term adverse effects remain challenging to determine. Traditional herbal medicine preparation methods are often labor-intensive, non-standardized, and face difficulties in identifying active ingredients. By improving medication development, optimization, and discovery procedures, Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides innovative ways to get beyond these restrictions. This systematic review aims to evaluate the role of AI-based software such as LEAFSNAP, Deep- Chem, PlantNet, Autodock, MestReNova, XCMS, ADMETlab, SynergyFinder, KEGG, TCMID, and Reactome in enhancing phytomedicine research by streamlining plant identification, bioactive compound discovery, molecular modeling, and pharmacokinetic profiling, thereby advancing drug discovery and development processes. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA guidelines) to explore the integration of AI-based tools in phytomedicine research and drug discovery. Literature searches were performed in Scopus, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases, focusing on studies published between January 2015 and January 2025. Only English-language articles focusing on AI-based software for drug discovery from plant-derived compounds were reviewed. Studies discussing synthetic drug development were excluded; this, along with non-English language, acted as a literature review limitation. Two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the retrieved articles. Any discrepancies in the screening, study selection, and data extraction processes were resolved through discussion and consensus. Through the effective identification of bioactive chemicals and the simplification of intricate studies, the combination of artificial intelligence and computer tools has completely transformed the process of discovering and developing herbal drugs. Artificial intelligence tools like ADMETlab for pharmacokinetics and toxicity assessments, DeepChem for molecular activity modelling, and AlphaFold for protein structure prediction have greatly improved the search for new herbal drugs. While AutoDock improves molecular docking simulations by automating ligand-receptor binding predictions for bioactive chemicals, LeafSnap and PlantNet make plant identification simpler. Drug development workflows are improved by databases such as KEGG and TC

title: Deep learning-accelerated contrast-enhanced 3D MRI for acute optic neuritis: faster acquisition and improved lesion conspicuity.
desc: [Frontiers in neurology] To compare a deep learning-accelerated contrast-enhanced 3D T1-weighted sequence (T1-CUBE-DLS) with standard parallel imaging-accelerated T1-CUBE for detecting acute optic neuritis (ON). This prospective study enrolled 59 patients with suspected acute ON (38 females; mean age 41.2 ± 12.8 years). All underwent contrast-enhanced whole-brain 3.0 T MRI including both T1-CUBE-DLS and standard T1-CUBE sequences. Two blinded neuroradiologists independently scored motion artifacts, subjective noise, and optic nerve clarity. Consensus readings recorded enhancement laterality, involved segments, and visual conspicuity. Enhancement length was measured per optic nerve, with inter-observer reliability assessed via intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis. Clinical diagnosis by a senior neuro-ophthalmologist served as the reference standard. Acute ON was confirmed in 43 of 59 patients (72.9%). T1-CUBE-DLS reduced acquisition time by 36.2%. Subjective noise was equivalent between sequences (p > 0.05), but T1-CUBE-DLS showed significantly fewer motion artifacts and superior optic nerve clarity (both p 0.05). T1-CUBE-DLS demonstrated stronger visual conspicuity (p = 0.011) and slightly longer measured enhancement length (mean difference, 0.836 mm; p < 0.0001). ICC for length measurement was 0.91 for T1-CUBE-DLS vs. 0.83 for standard T1-CUBE, with narrower 95% limits of agreement (-1.37 to 1.51 mm vs. - 3.1 to 2.4 mm). T1-CUBE-DLS reduces acquisition time by 36.2%, with no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy detected, while improving enhancement conspicuity and measurement reproducibility, supporting its potential as a practical and efficient alternative for ON evaluation.

title: Artificial intelligence across the cataract care continuum: a systematic scoping review introducing the CAICC framework and the surgical complexity prediction gap.
desc: [BMC ophthalmology] Cataracts remain a leading cause of reversible blindness, and artificial intelligence (AI) applications now span the cataract care pathway. However, the distribution of these applications and their validation maturity remain unclear. This review mapped AI across the care continuum, summarized task-specific performance, characterized validation maturity, and identified evidence gaps. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) was followed. PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, WorldCat, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology Meeting Archive were searched; the final search was completed on 20 July 2025. Eligible studies were English-language primary research published from 1 January 2020 through 20 July 2025. A review-specific cataract artificial intelligence clinical continuum (CAICC) evidence-mapping framework was developed during data charting and synthesis. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, endpoint adjudication, and validation-maturity assessment. Performance was summarized descriptively; validation maturity characterized evaluation independence and clinical stage, not risk of bias or overall methodological quality. Of 361 reports sought for retrieval, 122 (33.8%) were not retrieved; 113/122 (92.6%) were considered plausibly eligible from available metadata. The final synthesis included 185 studies: detection (n = 52), characterization (n = 50), personalized surgical planning (n = 27), intelligent surgery (n = 28), recovery (n = 24), and patient engagement (n = 4). Among 181 validation-applicable included studies, internal testing was the most frequent highest-maturity category (123/181, 68.0%), followed by external testing (33/181, 18.2%), prospective single-center evaluation (6/181, 3.3%), and prospective multicenter evaluation (2/181, 1.1%); 17/181 (9.4%) had no independent or unclear testing. Among the retrieved and included studies, no comprehensive clinically validated multimodal preoperative cataract surgical-complexity model was identified. Most included studies remained at internal validation stages, and prospective multicenter evaluation was rare. Because 122/361 reports sought for retrieval were unavailable and most were considered plausibly eligible, retrieval bias may affect the comprehensiveness of the evidence map. Future research should prioritize multimodal preoperative surgical-complexity prediction, independent external test

title: Artificial Intelligence for Predictive Microbiome Engineering: Integrating Community Design and Environmental Validation.
desc: [Environmental microbiology reports] Microbial ecosystems can now be measured across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and environmental dimensions, yet their emergent functions remain difficult to predict and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate heterogeneous data, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish causality, transferability, or controllability. This review developed a five-layer framework: observe, infer, predict, design, and learn that connects microbial measurement to prospective intervention and experimental feedback. We critically synthesise evidence from sequence and protein learning, multi-omics integration, metabolic modelling, synthetic microbial communities, environmental biotechnology, and temporal forecasting. Recent primary studies illustrate progress in forecasting community trajectories, predicting microbial competition and designing consortia for pollutant degradation; they also reveal important boundaries between model performance and demonstrated ecosystem control. We examine risks arising from compositional data, information leakage, dependent observations, batch effects, uncertain calibration, sparse perturbation data, ecological instability, and evolutionary change. We propose operational criteria for ecosystem programmability and a staged validation pathway from controlled systems to field-relevant environments. Progress will depend on standardised context-rich data, hybrid AI-mechanistic models, prospective benchmarks, independent replication, and safety-constrained design.

title: Development and Preliminary Validation of an AI-Derived Hemorrhage Metric for Surgical Skill Assessment in Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy.
source: PubMed · The Journal of surgical research
desc: [The Journal of surgical research] The objective assessment of technical skill remains a significant challenge in surgical training and quality control. Intraoperative hemorrhage, a direct consequence of tissue handling, may serve as a quantifiable proxy for surgical proficiency. This study aims to develop and validate an artificial intelligence-derived metric based on intraoperative hemorrhage for objective skill assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Frames were sampled at 1 fps (every 25th frame) from videos recorded at 25 fps, and the 70 curated cases were split at the video (case) level into training, validation, and test sets (8:1:1; 56/7/7 videos). An external test set included 30 cases from Zhujiang Hospital. Hemorrhagic regions were manually annotated on 84,680 frames from 56 training videos. A PoolNet-based model quantified hemorrhagic pixels per frame during critical view of safety. Model outputs were validated against surgeon assessments (Fleiss' κ = 0.72) and operative metrics, with the modified Global Operative Assessment of Laparoscopic Skills (mGOALS) scale as the skill reference. Mean hemorrhagic pixels were correlated with skill scores, ratings, and maneuver frequencies. The hemorrhage identification model achieved dice scores of 0.819 ± 0.054 (internal) and 0.685 ± 0.031 (external). The proficiency metric negatively correlated with expert skill scores (Spearman's r = -0.93, P < 0.001), and strongly positively with subjective bleeding assessments (ρ = 0.89, P < 0.001) and hemostasis frequency (ρ = 0.94, P < 0.001). It effectively stratified surgeons by skill, with high-skill operators having fewer hemorrhagic pixels (Kruskal-Wallis H = 21.0-31.1, P < 0.001). The developed model provides an objective, automated hemorrhage metric that, in this preliminary validation, aligned with expert skill ratings and operative behavior during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Pending difficulty-adjusted, multicentre validation, it may serve as a potential adjunct for postoperative, competency-based feedback rather than as a stand-alone measure of surgical skill.

title: Parent Perceptions of Virtual and Artificial Intelligence Scribes at Pediatric Medical Visits.
desc: [Applied clinical informatics] BACKGROUND: Scribes help physicians decrease electronic medical record documentation burden. There is transition from virtual to artificial intelligence (AI) scribes. A gap exists in our understanding of parent perspectives on technology-based scribe use at pediatric medical visits. OBJECTIVES: The objectives of this study were to explore parent perceptions of pediatric medical visits of lived experience with virtual scribe presence and consideration of hypothetical AI scribe use. METHODS: Semistructured qualitative interviews were conducted with parents of children aged 0 to 17 who visited 1 of 11 primary care pediatricians who worked with virtual scribes at a Midwestern clinic system. Parents were asked to reflect on visits with virtual scribe presence and their perceptions of hypothetical AI scribe use. Interviews were conducted by trained interviewers, recorded, and transcribed. Thematic analysis was applied to the transcripts using grounded theory and the constant comparative method. RESULTS: Interviews were completed by 33 parents, including 76% females, with a mean age of 40.30 years (standard deviation [SD] = 11.33). Two themes emerged regarding virtual scribe presence. First was that Parents felt heard, seen, and valued. Parents perceived greater focus and attention from the pediatrician. Second was Building trust in a third-party listener. Parents noted elements that built trust and overall low noticeability of scribe. Two themes emerged regarding hypothetical AI scribes. First was Valuing human information processing. Parents described concerns about AI accuracy and security and greater trust in human understanding. Second was AI as an Efficient workforce. Parents noted potential benefits for cost, reliability, and documentation. CONCLUSION: Parents described enhanced pediatrician connection at lived experience visits with virtual scribe presence. When considering hypothetical AI scribes, they perceived possible benefits but overall concerns for accuracy, security, and understanding. Studies of parents who experienced AI scribe presence at pediatric medical visits would be helpful to assess their perceptions of positive elements, benefits, and concerns.

title: Statistical Pitfalls in Large Language Model Evaluation: A Practical Guide to Study Design and Analysis.
desc: [Journal of clinical epidemiology] Studies evaluating large language models in medicine increasingly follow a common design in which a fixed set of clinical questions is posed to several sources, such as different language models, clinicians, or patient-education resources. The responses are then scored for outcomes including accuracy, completeness, readability, or similar measures. Because each source answers the same set of questions, the resulting observations are inherently paired: the question functions as the repeated unit across sources. Despite this structure, many studies analyze the resulting data using statistical procedures that assume independent observations. Treating paired observations as independent introduces a mismatch between the study design and the statistical analysis. In evaluations where multiple sources respond to the same questions, the responses are naturally correlated because they are influenced by shared characteristics of the question, such as difficulty or ambiguity. Ignoring this dependence can reduce statistical power and distort the nominal type I error rate. These issues arise when commonly used independent-sample procedures, including the Mann-Whitney test, the Kruskal-Wallis test, one-way analysis of variance, or unpaired t-tests, are applied to datasets generated from identical question sets. The appropriate analytical framework instead treats the question as the unit of pairing. Methods designed for repeated or paired observations, such as the Friedman test or repeated-measures analysis of variance for overall comparisons, followed by paired contrasts using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test or paired t-tests with appropriate multiplicity correction, provide analyses that align with the underlying design. Effect sizes and regression approaches that account for the paired structure, including mixed-effects models with question treated as a random effect, may further strengthen inference. Recognizing the repeated-measures nature of these evaluations provides a straightforward path toward more statistically coherent analyses.

title: Artificial Intelligence-driven Biomarker Discovery for Precision Psychiatry.
source: PubMed · Clinical psychopharmacology and neuroscience : the official scientific journal of the Korean College of Neuropsychopharmacology
desc: [Clinical psychopharmacology and neuroscience : the official scientific journal of the Korean College of Neuropsychopharmacology] Poor phenotype quality and small cohorts remain major constraints in psychiatric biomarker research, and recent methodological advances increasingly address them. Language models turn clinical text into analysable variables at a scale manual chart review cannot reach. Self-supervised models learn from the unlabelled signals psychiatry already collects. Variant-effect prediction makes molecular interpretation computable, and research agents have generated and experimentally confirmed candidates outside psychiatry. These capabilities act early, on what is measured, what can be learned from it and which candidates are proposed. None of the artificial intelligence capabilities reviewed here yet reaches the stages at which a candidate becomes a clinical test. Producing candidates is becoming cheap while qualifying them is not. This review is organised around that asymmetry rather than by disorder or marker catalogue. It separates the measured characteristic, the prediction model and the intended clinical use, and treats method family as distinct from evidential stage. Across the selected evidence, discrimination is supported more strongly in development data than in independent evaluation, and prospective evidence that model-guided use improves care is scarce. Many reported metrics also address a simpler task than the intended decision: diagnosis instead of differential diagnosis, general prognosis instead of differential treatment benefit. The review proposes a six-stage framework linking intended use, measurement validity, model evaluation, comparative utility and monitored deployment, and places each capability on it, clarifying where methodological progress can accelerate discovery and where conventional clinical validation remains indispensable.

title: Microbiome-driven precision psychiatry: integrating multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and personalized interventions along the gut-brain axis.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] This scoping review maps evidence for microbiome-driven precision psychiatry in depression and anxiety. Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE and PubMed Central from inception to July 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar and backward citation searching. Human primary studies were screened and charted; findings were synthesized narratively. Of 58 identified records, 49 remained after deduplication, 35 full texts were assessed, and 28 studies were included. The evidence was predominantly observational. Taxonomic findings varied across populations, while studies of microbial functions, metabolites, multi-omics signatures, and treatment response suggested potential for biological stratification. Microbiome-targeted interventions and artificial intelligence models remain exploratory. Microbiome-derived biomarkers and predictive models require standardized methods, independent validation, and prospective evidence of clinical utility before routine psychiatric use.

title: An interpretable deep learning framework for revealing fine-grained spatial domains.
desc: [Cell reports methods] Spatial transcriptomics enables gene expression profiling with preserved spatial context, yet accurate spatial domain delineation remains challenging. We present RIF, a robust and interpretable deep learning framework for fine-grained spatial domain identification. RIF leverages graph neural networks semi-supervised with pseudo-labels to preserve tissue structural integrity. It incorporates a dual-preprocessing ensemble strategy to improve model robustness and generalization. It further enables spatially variable gene detection through network interpretability. Across multiple sequencing platforms, RIF outperformed state-of-the-art comparison algorithms in spatial domain identification. In mouse brain tissue, RIF identified corresponding hippocampal subfields in the spatially separated dorsal and ventral regions and resolved the laminar organization of the olfactory bulb. In breast cancer, RIF-defined domains suggest suppressed T cell activity associated with hypoxic and oxidative microenvironments. In an invasive ductal carcinoma dataset of more than 720,000 cells, RIF-defined domains suggest an epithelial-mesenchymal transition gradient, including reduced hormone dependence and extracellular matrix remodeling.

title: An interpretable multimodal deep learning model for physiological stress detection.
desc: [PloS one] Stress is a major contributor to physical and mental health disorders, underscoring the need for reliable and interpretable detection systems. We present an interpretable multimodal deep learning framework that integrates electrocardiogram (ECG), electrodermal activity (EDA), and respiration signals using modality-specific neural architectures complemented by feature-based classical models. To ensure robustness and generalizability, the framework was evaluated under both subject-independent and subject-dependent protocols. Results show that multimodal fusion consistently outperformed single modalities, achieving 94.8% accuracy, 93.9% F1-score, and 0.97 AUC under subject-independent validation, compared with 86-91% accuracy for individual signals. In subject-dependent experiments, performance reached 97.2% accuracy and 96.8% F1-score. Comparative analysis with recent state-of-the-art methods demonstrated the competitiveness of our approach, while ablation studies confirmed the contribution of each modality and fusion strategy. Statistical significance testing with (p < 0.05) further validated the reliability of these gains. Importantly, interpretability analyses using Grad-CAM and attention visualization provided physiological insights, revealing that the model emphasizes clinically meaningful regions such as ECG R-peaks and phasic EDA fluctuations. By uniting high performance, robustness, and interpretability, this work advances stress detection research and offers a physiologically grounded framework for continuous mental health monitoring.

title: Artificial intelligence and its influence on student engagement in higher education.
desc: [Frontiers in psychology] Empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) relates to student engagement in culturally diverse higher-education settings remains limited. In Chinese university classrooms, where interaction is often teacher-led and asking questions in class can carry a social cost, AI-driven dialogic tools may offer low-pressure opportunities for active participation. This study examined the association between an AI conversational agent (EduBot) and the behavioural, cognitive, emotional and agentic dimensions of engagement among Chinese undergraduates. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design involved 555 students in four comprehensive (multi-disciplinary, research-intensive) universities, each contributing one introductory course taught in two parallel sections. Within a 15-week semester, intervention sections (n = 278) used EduBot, a Socratic-dialogue agent embedded in the learning management system, for 12 weeks; control sections (n = 277) used teaching-assistant-moderated forums. We measured engagement at three time points with a 21-item four-dimensional engagement scale adapted from an established measure and supplemented it with system logs, 30 student interviews and instructor focus groups. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for the nesting of students within course sections, together with mixed-design ANOVAs, showed Group × Time interactions for behavioural (η2p = 0.043, post-test d = 0.71), cognitive (η2p = 0.032, d = 0.55), agentic (η2p = 0.054, d = 0.57) and emotional engagement (η2p = 0.012, d = 0.34), all p ≤ 0.001 after Holm adjustment. Within the intervention group, the number of EduBot sessions predicted post-test engagement after adjustment for baseline scores and covariates. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated larger agentic gains among first-year students and larger cognitive gains among students with lower prior GPA. Thematic analysis identified three hypothesised mechanisms, namely a judgment-free interaction space, scaffolded persistence and temporal flexibility. A Socratic-scaffolded AI agent was associated with higher engagement, most clearly for agentic engagement, which participants described as constrained by classroom norms. The findings support culturally attentive AI design and suggest, tentatively, an equity-enhancing potential. Because the design compared an integrated AI package with usual practice across eight sections, the effects cannot be attributed to single design components.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Graph Methods for Microbiome Research: A Systematic Review.
desc: [WIREs mechanisms of disease] The complexity of high-throughput sequencing data in microbiome research necessitates advanced analytical methods to decipher microbial community structures and interactions. Graph-based methods, which model taxa as nodes and their relationships as edges, have emerged as a powerful framework for this purpose. However, the rapid evolution of these techniques, from classical network analysis to modern graph representation learning, has created a fragmented and complex methodological landscape. This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis and structured overview of the field. We systematically review the literature and propose a three-part classification to categorize the primary contribution of each study: (1) novel methods for microbial network representation, (2) applications of classical graph analysis, and (3) the emerging use of graph representation learning for predictive modeling. We summarize the most frequent applications within each class, including keystone species identification, community clustering, and graph-based disease classification. Furthermore, we identify critical cross-cutting challenges, such as the lack of standardized tools and the need for improved model interpretability. By structuring the current landscape of graph-based methods, this review serves as a crucial guide for researchers to select appropriate models and highlights key gaps to direct future research.

title: Artificial intelligence readiness in fragile states: a systematic review and theory-informed framework for workforce transformation in Somalia.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a determinant of national productivity and competitiveness, yet the conditions required for its beneficial adoption, infrastructure, institutions, and human capital, remain unevenly distributed across the globe. Somalia, a fragile and conflict-affected state undergoing a prolonged process of institutional reconstruction, exemplifies this unevenness: a young, digitally engaged population and a strikingly dynamic private telecommunications and mobile-money sector coexist with weak public institutions, fragmented higher education, and chronic graduate unemployment. This paper reports a systematic literature review with theory-informed framework development, conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, that synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence on organizational and national AI readiness, digital-skills development, and workforce productivity, with a specific focus on Somalia and comparable fragile, low-connectivity, Sub-Saharan African contexts. Using the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and human capital theory as complementary lenses, the review synthesizes findings from 31 sources identified through a structured search and screening process. The evidence indicates that Somalia's AI readiness gap is not primarily a technological deficit but a multidimensional one, spanning fragmented digital infrastructure, weak institutional governance and data ecosystems, a persistent mismatch between higher-education curricula and labour-market needs, and the absence of coordinated national AI or digital-skills policy. Building on these findings, the paper proposes a four-pillar conceptual AI readiness framework intended to guide future empirical assessment and policy discussion, encompassing digital infrastructure and access, institutional and governance readiness, human capital and skills development, and labour-market integration, together with a phased implementation roadmap for government, higher-education institutions, the private telecommunications sector, and development partners. The review provides a literature-grounded, context-specific synthesis of AI readiness for a fragile Horn of Africa state and offers a transferable analytical approach for similar settings.

title: Local processors: Active dendrites and artificial intelligence.
desc: [Current research in neurobiology] Neuroscience and artificial intelligence have been closely connected for over a century, with each field influencing the other. Modern artificial intelligence systems rely almost exclusively on the point-neuron model, where inputs are linearly summed and passed through a global activation function. Although highly successful, this architecture differs substantially from neural computation that occurs in the brain, and current leading models require massive infrastructure consuming megawatts of power, which contrasts to the brain's remarkable efficiency. One underexplored source of biologically inspired computational principles lies in the dendrites of pyramidal neurons. This review examines the electrical properties of active dendrites and how they could inform the next generation of artificial intelligence architectures. We describe how dendrites can function as semi-independent computational subunits, generating local nonlinear events that implement coincidence detection, signal amplification, and logical operations within a single neuron. We discuss how the structural segregation of different dendritic compartments provides a biologically grounded alternative to global error backpropagation through local credit assignment. We further examine how activity-dependent spine growth and pruning support continual learning without catastrophic forgetting, and how the spatiotemporal selectivity of dendritic integration gives rise to sparse, energy-efficient representations. Together, dendritic computation represents a potential blueprint for artificial intelligence architectures that are adaptive, context-aware, and energetically frugal.
